Apple and other tech giants may have to make an annual lump-sum payment to the EU under a revised digital services tax plan.

The EU wants to raise revenue through a revised version of an earlier proposal without angering the White House…

Disputes over digital services taxes among EU member states have dragged on for years. For Apple, the services in question include iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV and Apple Creator Studio, among others.

Critics point out that these companies earn enormous revenues selling subscriptions to European users yet pay no tax on those earnings in Europe. Others worry that a digital levy would disproportionately hit European firms; still others fear the White House will threaten retaliation if US companies are hit with extra taxes.

The Financial Times reports that the European Commission has now put forward a compromise designed to please everyone — except, of course, the companies like Apple, Google and Meta that would be paying the new levy.

Officials say Brussels is considering tweaking an existing proposal that would require every business operating in the EU with annual revenue above €100m to pay a flat annual fee… Adjusting the thresholds and payment amounts under the Core scheme so that it only catches the very largest companies would both raise more tax from tech groups and soften European criticism that the Core scheme would sweep up large numbers of mid-sized European businesses, officials said.

The revised plan would not single out companies selling digital services, but would apply to all large companies. Since it was the earlier proposal that triggered White House threats of retaliatory tariffs, the EU hopes the new version will not spark a fresh trade war with the US.

The most upvoted comment was posted by cubbuc

I'm not against taxing big tech. But we have to be clear that at this point we have to accept that companies capable of growing big simply don't get born in Europe; and if they do, our limp-wristed regulators are incapable of stopping them from being bought up by American giants.

You can keep playing this game of cat and mouse with US tech companies, but you will always lose.

Or you could actually start doing the hard work and address what is clearly a structural and systemic problem across the continent.

Exactly how much each company would pay has not been finalised. The plan is to first reach agreement in principle among the 27 EU member states before deciding on the rate.

9to5Mac Opinion

This mess was supposed to be sorted out by a global agreement brokered through the OECD. That agreement would have ensured every company in the world paid at least some tax in every country in which it operated, and Apple had said it supported it.

However, Donald Trump pulled the US out of that agreement, and voices were raised demanding an EU-only version. The idea that Trump wouldn't object to this revised version sounds, to me, dangerously optimistic.
